text: The Reserves can then remain invested to generate returns.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are studying this carefully and discussing it with the President and the Council of Presidential Advisers.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Through both saving ahead and borrowing, we expect to smooth out and be able to meet our major infrastructure needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For healthcare, security and other social spending, the increases will be recurrent, will benefit Singaporeans broadly, and will directly benefit current generations.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The responsible way to pay for them is through taxation so that every generation pays its share.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The exact timing will depend on the state of the economy, how much our expenditures grow, and how buoyant our existing taxes are.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But I expect that we will need to do so earlier rather than later in the period.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This GST increase is necessary because even after exploring various options to manage our future expenditures through prudent spending, saving and borrowing for infrastructure, there is still a gap.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This boost in revenue will be vital in closing this gap.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will continue to manage our expenditures and the need for other future revenue measures carefully, and plan ahead early for our overall revenue and expenditure needs.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will implement the GST increase in a progressive manner, as we have always done in the past.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: First, we will continue to absorb GST on publicly-subsidised education and healthcare.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Second, we will enhance the permanent GST Voucher (GSTV) scheme when the GST is increased, so as to provide more help to lower-income households and seniors.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, we already disburse about $800 million per year from the GSTV Fund.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This year, we will make a $2 billion top-up to the GSTV Fund to support these payments.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Third, we will also implement an offset package for a period to help Singaporeans adjust to the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Lower- and middle-income households will receive more support.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will provide more details once we have determined the timing of the GST increase.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we mention the need to raise taxes, a natural question is: why do we not tap more on our Reserves instead?

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Indeed, we have been doing so over the last decade.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I mentioned earlier that we introduced the NIR framework in 2008.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This started out with the Reserves managed by the Government of Singapore Investment Corporation (GIC) and the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS).

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Temasek was then included in the framework in 2015.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Through this framework, we now spend on the basis of total returns on our Reserves, including both realised and unrealised capital gains.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are able to supplement our revenues with NIRC today because our predecessors judiciously set aside the savings from the strong growth during Singapore’s earlier stage of economic development.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Now that our economy is maturing, and our population is ageing, we must husband this resource carefully, prudently and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This allows our Reserves to grow with our economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: If instead, we used 100% of the returns, the principal sum of the Reserves will stagnate over time, and the NIRC, as a share of GDP, will consequently fall as our economy grows.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The impact of this will not be trivial, given that our Budget now relies on the NIRC as our largest source of revenue.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In a more extreme scenario, if we spent more than our investment returns, we will eat into our nest egg.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Doing so would mean that our Reserves will shrink over time, generating a progressively smaller stream of income in the years that follow, till eventually our Reserves are exhausted.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We must also never forget that, as an island nation with no hinterland and no natural resources, our Reserves lend long-term stability to our economy and afford us the means to weather crises.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: During the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis, our Reserves and strong economic fundamentals kept the Singapore dollar stable even as currency speculators were attacking other regional currencies.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: During the 2008 Global Financial Crisis, our Reserves anchored our economy against the storm by backing a $150 billion guarantee for all bank deposits in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: And during the recession in 2009, our Reserves funded a total of $4 billion for the Jobs Credit Scheme and Special Risk-Sharing Initiative to help employers and employees tide over the difficult period.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: As a small and open economy, we will always be vulnerable to fluctuations in the global economy and financial markets.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We can never predict where or when the next crisis will come.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we know, when the next crisis hits, we will be able to weather the storm because we have our Reserves.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I will now introduce other changes to make our tax system more progressive, fair and resilient.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: One common suggestion is to tax the rich and higher-income more or introduce wealth taxes like a capital gains tax.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This reflects a desire for a progressive system, with those with more contributing back to society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This is fair and is precisely what we have done over the years.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We increased personal income tax rates for our top income brackets in 2015 and imposed a cap on personal income tax reliefs in 2016.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, our BSD rates for residential properties range between 1% and 3% and have remained unchanged since 1996.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The new top marginal rate of 4% will apply to the portion of residential property value which is in excess of $1 million.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This change will apply to all residential properties acquired from tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The BSD rates for non-residential properties remain unchanged at 1% to 3%  .

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Moving forward, we will continue to study options to ensure that our tax system remains progressive.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Today, services, such as consultancy and marketing, purchased from overseas suppliers are not subject to GST.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Local consumers also do not pay GST when they download apps and music from overseas.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This change will ensure that imported and local services are accorded the same treatment  .

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For the import of goods, there are international discussions on how GST can apply.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We will review this before deciding on the measure to take.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I will also be extending and strengthening other tax incentives to enhance our business competitiveness in this Budget.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The details of these changes are in the Annex  .

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Expenditure in many areas will rise, especially in healthcare, infrastructure and security.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To meet these needs, we must plan ahead and prepare early.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We need to remain prudent in our spending, save up where possible, and raise revenues, but in a fair and progressive way.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This way, we can ensure a fiscally sustainable and secure future for ourselves and our children.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Having laid out our plans to prepare for the next decade, let me now cover our overall Budget position for the near term.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: For FY2017, we expect an overall Budget surplus of $9.6 billion or 2.1% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We do not expect either to occur every year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We cannot base our long-term fiscal planning on the basis of exceptional factors being positive, year after year.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: I will, therefore, use some of this year’s exceptional surplus to save ahead for future spending.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This will help to pay for the new rail lines that we are building.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: The SG Bonus will cost the Government $700 million  .

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It reflects the Government’s long-standing commitment to share the fruits of Singapore’s development with Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Notwithstanding the overall Budget surplus, the FY2017 Budget remains expansionary for the domestic economy.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: When we exclude NIRC and top-ups to funds, we expect a basic deficit of $1 billion, or 0.2% of GDP.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: In FY2018, our Budget position will remain expansionary.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Ministries’ total expenditures are expected to be $80 billion, or 8.3% higher than in FY2017.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: To prepare for this Budget, I spoke to many businesses, organisations, community partners, and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: They gave me useful feedback, which helped refine our policies and set our priorities for the years ahead.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Budget 2018 is about laying the foundation for our nation's development in the next decade.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It seeks to support our transformation into a vibrant and innovative economy, by fostering pervasive innovation, building deep capabilities and forging strong partnerships.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It seeks to build a smart, green and liveable city, so that Singaporeans can enjoy a high-quality living environment.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It also seeks to further our collective efforts to foster a caring and cohesive society, by harnessing the sense of community and the spirit of giving in our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: At its heart, the Budget is a strategic and integrated financial plan to position Singapore for the future.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: It is a means for us to achieve the aspirations of our people, a roadmap for us to achieve our vision for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Our path ahead will not be easy, especially in light of the major shifts happening around us – a changing global economic landscape, the emergence of new technologies, and our own demographic transition.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: But we have confronted graver challenges in the past and have always been able to overcome them, using our wits and relying on the solidarity of our people.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We are now in a much stronger position than we have been in the past.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: We have a diversified and well-connected economy, a highly motivated and educated workforce, a cohesive and resilient society.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Together, we will marshal our resources and chart our course – to come together, to work together, to make our aspirations today the reality tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: This way, we can build a better Singapore for everyone.

speaker: Mr Heng Swee Keat
text: Together, we can make a better future for all of us.
